The marine propeller shaft experiences various dynamic disturbances due to shifts in hydrodynamic forces, shaft speed variations, external misalignment forces, shaft bow, harmonic forces of the reciprocating engines 1 , and bore misalignment 2 .Large hydrodynamic forces are generated particularly during maneuvers such as turning when inflow to the propeller changes rapidly inducing vibration and bending moment 3 .These, in turn, affect the bending parameters of the propeller shaft system, manifested in increased bearing reaction and shaft curvature or slope within the main bearings and vibration magnitude 1 .Traditionally stern tubes and intermediate bearings are typically designed for specific operating conditions and the initial setting of the bearing height, which influences the radial clearance subsequently affecting the bearing hydrodynamic characteristics, is based on the shaft and bearing bending performance in terms of bearing reaction force and the shaft slope at the support points as required by the rules and regulations of the classification societies.For instance, American Bureau of Shipping rules 4 emphasize the importance of accounting for hull deflections and bearing reactions across varied conditions, including cold and hot static states, as well as ballast versus fully loaded drafts Similarly, Det Norske Veritas (DNV) requires alignment calculations during critical phases of cold static, hot static, and hot running with hydrodynamic loads placing particular emphasis on the influence of hull deflections.DNV technical reports also highlight that aft bearing damage can occur during operation with partial propeller immersion because of the eccentric thrust forces inducing downward shaft bending, which leads to edge loading and localized overheating 5 .Simulations confirm this, showing that partial immersion increases both the bearing reaction force and the journal slope.It is clear that static-based bearing height settings lack the capacity for real-time vertical adjustments which can result in bearing overload and excessive shaft slope when dynamic situations are not within the design envelop of the static setting of the bearing height underscoring the need for an automatic bearing height adjustment of the main bearings of marine propeller shafts 6 .The theory of adjusting the bearing radial clearance is fundamentally connected to rotordynamics, as altering the bearing clearance impacts the direct and quadrature stiffness components, thereby influencing the response of the bearing-rotor system [7][8][9] .Adjustable features of the hydrodynamic journal bearings can be used to alter the shaft-bearing interaction, and in cases where the shaft is supported by more than two bearings the reaction force of the adjusted bearing can be manipulated to significantly enhance stability in marine gearboxes 10 and real-time alignment in high-speed turbines to ensuring stability 11 .

To achieve the adjustable features of the hydrodynamic bearings, several approaches are used, including controlled oil injection in active lubrication in tilting-pad bearings 12 and in thrust bearings, addressing vibration transmission challenges 13 .Magnetorheological lubricants are used with active magnetic field control to enhance the stiffness and carrying capacity of the oil film in hydrodynamic bearings 9 .Furthermore, active magnetic bearings used adaptive control with nonlinear observers for computing nonlinear control currents 14,15 and incorporating advanced modeling and experimental validation techniques [16][17][18] .For the control strategy, a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) is used with extended state observers effectively suppresses torsional vibration compared to PID controllers, achieving superior control outcomes 19,20 even in the case of mass uncertainties 21 and when coupled with active control systems incorporating LQR-guided damping absorbers and electromagnetic actuators outperform passive controls in managing displacement, deflection, and velocity in complex systems 22 .Performance-wise, actively controlled journal bearings enhance stability by up to six times compared to non-controlled systems, utilizing parametric excitation to optimize radial clearance control 23 .

In the case of the marine propeller shaft system, the bearings are located on elastic supports to include the hull deformation effect.To compensate for this support flexibility, actuators can be inserted between the hull and the bearings.For example, electromagnetic actuators significantly reduce rotor vibration in maneuvering vehicles and seismic-exposed rotor-shaft systems 24,25 with a semi-solid viscoelastic model to address lateral vibration problems 26 and improve vibration isolation in naval equipment 27 , diesel generators 28 , thrust bearings 29 and managing sub-synchronous vibration in moving base rotor systems 30,31 .

32 investigated the effectiveness of a PZT-actuated controller on a test rig, demonstrating significant vibration suppression.Under a 40 N step load, the controlled system exhibited a substantial reduction in vibration amplitude compared to the uncontrolled case.At 5000 rpm, the vibration amplitude at the shaft end decreased from 1.45 μm to a lower value.A similar trend was observed at 10,000 rpm.Furthermore, the control strategy significantly improved response time, with vibration decay time at 5000 rpm decreasing from 0.38 s to as low as 0.02 s in the controlled system.These results underscore the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy in achieving rapid vibration suppression and precise control of the rotor-bearing actuator system.

For a more precise bearing elevation, piezoelectric actuators are used, for example, in gyroscopic rotor systems to minimize rotor displacement without increasing bearing forces 33 , reducing lateral vibrations at critical speeds in rotor-bearing systems 34 , and attenuating vibrations across multiple modes in plate-like structures 35 .For low-frequency problems often associated with hull deformation issues, hydraulic actuated journal bearings 36 , variable impedance bearings 37 , deformable bushings 38 , and journal bearings with flexible sleeves 39 have been shown to enhance rotor stability and vibration control 40 .In all of the reviewed systems above, no application of automatic bearing height adjustment to control propeller shaft bending parameters has been reported.This paper proposes a system for automatically adjusting the vertical offset of bearing housings and presents an analysis of rotor bending parameters and vibration responses for low-speed marine shafts where direct adjustment of minute radial clearances is impractical.This approach, especially under static or quasi-static conditions, uses bearing and slope influence coefficients to determine the propeller shaft response for a given unit of displacement of the bearing.
System modeling

A marine propeller shaft system of a single stern tube bearing is shown in Fig. 1 where the rotor is supported by a stern tube bearing (STB), an intermediate bearing (IB), and engine bearings.The single stern tube bearing design is selected in this analysis due to its noisier, more frequent failures and challenging shaft alignment process 41 , where the conventional practice of aligning propulsion shafts is insufficient and a special method is required 42 .

To satisfy the propeller shaft bending parameters limits in complying with the classification societies' rules and regulations, it is necessary to determine those parameters, and this can be achieved by adjusting the bearing initial elevation, z 0 (also known as the bearing offset from the shaft centerline axis) of either the intermediate bearing.or the engine bearings or both, which can be derived from the Bearing Influence Coefficients (BIC) and Slope Influence Coefficients (SIC) matrices 43 .The dynamic behavior of a marine propeller shafting system subjected to base excitation of hull deformation is investigated.A mathematical model is developed using state space to study the effect of an automatic bearing offset adjustment system on the response of the shaft and casing vibration of the intermediate bearing, including its bending parameters.

The equations govern how the pedestal (connected rigidly to the bearing housing) YB moves vertically, considering its connections to both the shaft YB and the hull Y Hull.The motion of the bearing housing is influenced by the relative velocities and displacements of the connected components, governed by the respective damping and stiffness coefficients.

The use of state-space matrices allows the incorporation of multi-frequency disturbances and control forces.This approach simplifies control performance evaluation by enabling displacement observation and slope constraint management without relying on the Lagrangian method.Practical constraints, such as ease of access and cost, dictate that the actuator for the automatic bearing offset control system is to be located at the intermediate bearing.Figure 2 depicts an intermediate bearing of a marine propeller shaft equipped with a proximity probe to measure shaft displacement in the vertical direction and a load cell or pressure sensor to monitor bearing force.The load cell provides a reaction force monitoring system, ensuring the force stays within the bearing load limit.The bearing is mounted on an actuator, either piezoelectric or hydraulic, which adjusts the vertical elevation of the bearing housing to maintain the journal slope of the stern tube bearing within ± 0.3 mrad 4 .

The active bearing adjustment system, as shown in Fig. 2, evaluates the control of the stern tube bearing slope through fine adjustments of the intermediate bearing elevation.The system comprises a shafting arrangement, a vertically adjustable bearing housing with a load cell, and two pairs of proximity probes positioned along the STB and the intermediate bearing.

The actuator measures the dynamic load of the intermediate bearing based on hydraulic pressure or load cell data, while the journal slope of the stern tube is monitored using proximity probes under various operational states, including afloat hot, hydrodynamic, or bearing wear conditions.The system also mitigates vertical perturbations caused by hull vibrations transmitted through the bearings.

Since the hold-down bolts of the intermediate bearing housing to the hull girder prevent any meaningful movement and allow the relative movement of the intermediate bearing to the shaft, the bearing structure incorporates Belleville springs and actuators to provide the necessary force for elevation adjustment.Belleville springs provide preload for consistent contact pressure and stiffness, enabling controlled vertical displacement (Y bearing ) and still providing the necessary passive stiffness in case of power failure.A proximity probe measures the shaft displacement relative to the bearing housing, and a load cell provides the force acting on the bearing.The force reading on the bearing can also be used to experimentally determine the bearing-shaft pair stiffness.

By modifying the vertical elevation of the intermediate bearing, the actuator influences the casing response of the intermediate bearing (Y bearing ) as well as the response of the intermediate and tail shafts (Y shaft ).In this context, Y Hull represents the deformation of the hull alongside the disturbance arising from dynamic conditions such as sailing in calm open water, turning, or maneuvering the vessel.

Figure 3 illustrates the working principle of the adjustable bearing offset system.If the slope across the stern tube bearing exceeds the allowable limit, a controller activates an actuator to adjust the bearing housing elevation to the desired vertical offset.This closed-loop control process continuously adjusts the bearing vertical offset until optimal slope and reaction forces are achieved.Considering the force generated by the actuator within the controlled system, the equations of motion of the propulsion shafting system can be expressed as follows:

Criteria for corrective force calculation

The key variables included in the adjustment function should adhere to the constrained optimization process 43 , which involves equality, inequality, and ordering constraints, and must fulfill the following criteria:

• Alignment Reference: It serves as the baseline or alignment reference; this implies that the vertical offset of the stern tube bearings must be zero.• Net Downward Loading: It is essential to ensure that the net downward loading on all the bearings is not excessive to achieve an elastic curve condition.Excessive loading can perturb the slope at the main bearings and lead to edge loading, • Slope constraint.

The slope of each elastic curve at the bearing location should not exceed the limit of ± 0.3 mrad.(7)   where: This force is needed to bring the journal slope at the stern tube bearing to the desired limits.The coefficient BICIB−IB represents the degree to which the intermediate bearing affects its reaction force when the bearing elevation is adjusted vertically.A higher coefficient signifies that more force is needed to achieve the same vertical elevation.Moreover, the coefficient SICIB−ST B is a coupled coefficient that measures how sensitive the stern tube bearing is to the changes made at the intermediate bearing.Mechanically, this reflects how adjustments at the intermediate bearing propagate through the shaft system and impact the stern tube bearing.If the system is tightly coupled with a high magnitude of the coefficient, even a small adjustment at the intermediate bearing will have a significant effect on the stern tube bearing.

For instance, the studies by 38,45 on the impact of bearing elevation on the natural frequency of marine propeller shafts highlighted the critical role of considering both bearing load and journal slope simultaneously when determining bearing vertical offset.This integrated approach, according to their findings, significantly enhances bearing performance.Specifically, a reduction in one bearing's offset to -9 mm resulted in an improved load ratio of 2.92 and a calculated angle of 0.132 mrad.These results strongly suggest that optimizing bearing design requires a careful consideration of both load and slope factors.
The controlling model

The bearing influence coefficient of the intermediate bearing on itself (BIC IB−IB ) can be determined experimentally by comparing the bearing reaction force at zero offset to the bearing reaction after lowering the intermediate bearing by 1 mm.

As demonstrated in Fig. 1, the purpose of the pair of proximity probes across the stern tube bearing is to measure the effect of a 1 mm adjustment of the intermediate bearing on the slope of the stern tube bearing (SIC IB−ST B ) as well as the slope at the stern tube bearing.Whilst the pair of proximity probes across the intermediate bearing (Y 3 and Y 4 ) is only a controlling measure, the slope across the intermediate bearing will not exceed the limits of the classification societies.

Methodology

The methodology initiated with modeling the shaft arrangement using a stiffness matrix approach to derive the global stiffness matrix and compute the influence coefficients (BIC) and (SIC).The main physical parameters used in the model shown in Fig. 2, such as shaft stiffness, mass, damping, and bearing, are listed in Table 1.These values are used for the development of the mass, stiffness, and damping matrices.Subsequent model validation was conducted as described in 43 .The validated model was then represented in state-space form.This representation facilitated the investigation of controlled system behavior under various input disturbances.By incorporating an actively controlled actuator at the intermediate bearing, the control objective was to regulate the journal slope of the stern tube bearing within acceptable limits through the application of corrective forces.
Definitions and assumptions

1. Reference line: The centerline passing through the center of the aft end of the propeller shaft is considered a reference point, where all the bearing offsets are referred to.2. The radial clearance of the intermediate bearing, with a 440 mm diameter, was considered to be 2 mils per inch of shaft diameter, with a total diametral clearance of around 1.78 to 2.0 mm, 3. Bearings are defined as single support points located at the mid-span of each bearing length, except the stern tube bearing, where the support point of 1/3 the shaft diameter forward from the aft end of the bearing is specified.where T 0 and Q 0 are the thrust and torque, respectively, calculated based on the technical specs of the driving engine 43 .Hydrodynamic loads on a marine propeller are influenced by several factors, primarily the direction of propeller rotation within the wake-field generated by the hull.The wake field itself is a non-uniform inflow velocity field, due to the complex interactions between the shape of the hull and the water.The hydrodynamic load data are normally calculated using a model or based on computational fluid dynamics.The operational loads in this paper were calculated using a set of empirical equations at maximum continuous rating and zero rudder angle 46 and cited in 43 .

Influence coefficient calculation necessitates measuring the bending parameters of the shafting arrangement when the vertical offset is at a known predefined vertical displacement.Therefore, the bearing reaction force at the intermediate bearing and the journal slope at both bearings are typically measured at a 0 mm offset under any operating state.To determine the nominal corrective force that is needed by the actuator, the process begins by computing the corresponding bending parameters V 0 , S 0 , and M 0 .Next, the influence coefficient matrices for slope (SIC), reaction force (BIC), and bending moment (MIC) are calculated.The slope limit is then determined
Parameter Value Units

Stiffness of the propeller shaft ( Ks) ) and the bearing influence coefficient (BIC IB−IB ) are extracted.Based on these, corrective measures are calculated by determining the relative slope to the slope limit and the corrective vertical force required to be applied on IB.Finally, the bearing vertical offset is updated, and the bearing parameters are recalculated to reflect the corrected slope.The results are then verified to ensure they comply with the bounding limits set by marine standards.The stern tube bearing, being generally inaccessible and its offset is unadjustable, serves as the reference point for aligning the shaft arrangement.The slope at the stern tube bearing can be indirectly adjusted by repositioning the intermediate bearing.The following calculates the bearing parameters of the propeller shaft system and determines the corrective force required for the intermediate bearing if the slope at the stern tube bearing exceeds the acceptable limits.The adjustment involves a propeller shafting arrangement of Fig. 1, with vertical offsets constrained between 0 mm and − 5 mm for downward loading and elastic curve criteria.The alignment curve is recalculated to distribute reaction forces among bearings, ensure the propeller shaft slope remains within permissible limits, and minimize the bending moment (Fig. 3).
Active control using PID

A PID controller with a disturbance observer and active control has been implemented to actively adjust the vertical offset of the intermediate bearing in a marine propeller shaft.This ensures that the journal slope of the stern tube bearing remains within specified limits.The PID controller uses the difference between the current and desired stern tube bearing slopes as its feedback signal.This error is processed to calculate the appropriate control signal.The initial slope is set by the slope block as shown in Fig. 4. The gains of the controller (proportional, integral, and derivative) are initially set to 8.0 × 10 4 , 200, and 50, respectively.These gains amplify the incoming signal to the PID controller.The controller calculates the control signal based on these components and adjusts the intermediate bearing vertical offset.

The controller gains are optimized to minimize steady-state error.It is important to note that the controller utilizes relevant influence coefficients from the BIC and SIC matrices, which are part of the marine propeller shaft stiffness matrix.These coefficients help establish the relationship between bearing offsets and slopes.
Results and discussion

This section presents the results of journal slope within the intermediate and stern tube bearings for both controlled and uncontrolled systems.Subsequently, the response of the system to various disturbance inputs is examined in the absence of actuator force.Finally, the actuator force generated by the controller is utilized along with the input disturbance to adjust the elevation of the intermediate bearing.Housing.This adjustment effectively regulates the slope within the stern tube bearing.
Validation of the model

While comprehensive testing under various hull loadings is paramount, the mathematical approach was initially verified using the seagoing conditions.By applying the calculated hydrodynamic loads on the propeller, as demonstrated in 43 , this is to mimic the operating conditions of the medium range tanker, and using the initial calculated offsets from 42 .The journal slope at the stern tube bearing was found to exceed the acceptable limit of 0.501 mrad, Table 3, as well as the bearing reaction forces specified in 4 and presented in Table 2.
Stability analysis

The root locus of the system demonstrates stable operation to the left of the vertical axis of the complex plane, where the vertical axis represents the damped natural frequency, ω d (rad/s).Input signals and disturbances result in vibrations that decay over time in this stable region.The parametric stability analysis was conducted by iterating over multiple ranges of key system parameters, including K B , C B and rotational speed (Ω).For each parameter combination, the state-space matrix A was constructed to capture the coupled dynamics of the primary mass and the bearing housing, with rotational effects incorporated by subtracting a term proportional to Ω from the matrix.The eigenvalues of the state-space matrix were computed for each parameter set and plotted in the complex plane.The real part of the eigenvalues indicates the system growth or decay rates, while the imaginary part corresponds to the damped natural frequency.This iterative approach maps the stability boundaries as the mechanical properties and rotational speeds vary, offering a comprehensive visualization of the system's dynamic behavior and stability characteristics.

Figure 5 illustrates the complete root locus of the system under varying bearing radial clearances (0.1-2.0 mm) and shaft rotational speeds ranging from 30 to 200 RPM.The marker shapes distinguish different speed levels, while the marker colors represent clearance values.The vertical red dashed line at δ = 0 denotes the stability boundary between the left half-plane (stable) and the right half-plane (unstable).The gray markers indicate all computed poles from the system equations, capturing the full eigenvalue spectrum.The poles, which govern the transient behavior, are overlaid using colored markers.A noticeable rightward shift of the poles with increasing clearance reflects a reduction in system stability.

This subplot, at the bottom left, provides a magnified view of the poles located near the imaginary axis, extracted from the complete eigenvalue set.The plot highlights the sensitivity of the pole locations to changes in bearing clearance and shaft speed.As the clearance increases, the poles migrate rightward.This movement toward the imaginary axis signals reduced stability margins, though all poles remain within the stable region.Table 2.The reaction force at each bearing for the controlled and uncontrolled method

The 3D surface plot, at bottom right, complements the root locus diagrams by providing a continuous representation of the real part of the poles across the parametric space.presents the real part of the pole as a function of bearing clearance and shaft speed.It demonstrates the trend observed in the root locus plots as clearance increases; the real part of the pole becomes less negative, indicating reduced system stability.The surface shows a consistent increase in the real part with larger clearances, especially at higher speeds.Although the real parts remain negative throughout the evaluated space.
Application of the active controller

The primary objective of using active control is to correct the misalignment of the journal slope caused by external disturbances.By continuously monitoring the slope of the stern tube bearing and intermediate bearing, the active control system applies corrective force at the intermediate bearing to bring the slope of the stern tube bearing within specified tolerance limits, ensuring optimal performance and minimizing the risk of an edge-free loading condition.Besides, the active control responds to external disturbances of vibration, hull deformation, and other varying hydrodynamic load conditions that cannot be eliminated.
Response of the controller

The dynamic response of the controller to a variety of disturbance inputs, including step, impulse, and sinusoidal waveforms, demonstrates its stability, transient behavior, and disturbance rejection capabilities.Sinusoidal disturbances with random noise effectively simulate periodic environmental forces during sailing, capturing wave-induced oscillations and stochastic turbulence effects 47 Impulse disturbances, on the other hand, are ideal for analyzing system responses to abrupt inputs, such as sudden maneuvers or direction changes 48,49 making them crucial for maritime navigation and control system evaluation.

Marine propeller shafts are subjected to various external forces and moments, leading to two primary types of input disturbances: step and sinusoidal.Step inputs, characterized by sudden and sustained changes, can arise from abrupt engine power variations, impacts from external obstructions, or sudden changes in water density or flow speed.These events can cause rapid increases or decreases in propeller thrust, leading to significant stresses on the shaft.Additionally, changes in shaft stiffness due to wear, thermal expansion, structural deformation, or misalignment can also contribute to step input disturbances.

In contrast, sinusoidal input disturbances represent periodic variations in external forces.These include waveinduced forces, where the regular oscillation of waves transmits cyclic forces to the propeller and subsequently the shaft.Propeller imbalance or misalignment, resulting from uneven mass distribution or slight angular deviations, can also induce cyclic lateral forces.Furthermore, engine-induced vibrations, often exhibiting harmonic characteristics, contribute to these periodic disturbances.The vertical displacements Y 1 and Y 2 , and Y B measured by the proximity probes capture the shaft deformation, incorporating the effect of hull-induced deflection and any additional dynamic effects arising during operation.By including real-time measurements of the actual shaft displacement within the STB as well as the vertical displacement of the IB, the proposed approach offers a more accurate basis for bearing adjustment, accounting for the combined effects of static and dynamic shaft response 50 .

As demonstrated in Fig. 6, in response to a step input, the system exhibits an overshoot of approximately 20% before settling to its steady-state value within 6.8 s over 10 s simulation window.This overshoot signifies the transient response characteristics, indicating the maximum deviation from the steady-state value.Conversely, an impulse input, characterized by its sudden, transient nature, elicits a more pronounced overshoot of approximately 35%.However, the system recovers more rapidly, settling within 4.5 s.The sinusoidal disturbance response provides insights into the controller's dynamic tracking and rejection capabilities.The continuous, periodic nature of the input disturbance results in a phase lag and potential amplitude attenuation in the output, contingent upon the system's damping characteristics.The overshoot is generally lower for sinusoidal disturbances, approximately 15%, due to the steady-state nature of the input.The ability to maintain stable oscillations or suppress vibrations becomes the primary performance metric.
Effectiveness of using the controller for the automatic adjustment of the vertical offset

To assess the effectiveness of using a coupled equation involving the SIC of the stern tube bearing and the BIC of the intermediate bearing for adjusting the vertical offset of the intermediate bearing and minimizing the constrained journal slope of the stern tube bearing under operational conditions, calculated bending parameters were compared.These comparisons involved comparing the initial calculated offsets from 42 to the adjusted offsets resulting from applying a controlled force at the intermediate bearing.

The results, illustrated in Fig. 7 and tabulated in Tables 3 and 5, demonstrate that combining the SIC of the stern tube bearing with the BIC of the intermediate bearing in computing the required adjusting offset significantly reduces the slope at the stern tube bearing.This mechanism led to adjusting the vertical offset of the intermediate bearing by raising the bearing housing by 0.852 mm, maintaining the ordering constraints of the bearings of the propeller shaft.

Applying the equations outlined in Sects.(2.2) and (3.1), in conjunction with the influence coefficients calculated under operational loads, reveals that a corrective force of 20.65 kN is necessary to adjust the vertical offset of the intermediate bearing.This adjustment increases the reaction force at the intermediate bearing and correspondingly decreases it at the stern tube bearing.

The mathematical approach was further verified under different conditions: cold dry-docked, hot afloat with the impeller fully immersed, and hot afloat with 70% immersion.The results are illustrated in Fig. 7 and detailed for each condition in Tables 4, 5 and 6.

Table 6 illustrates the calculated bearing reaction forces for the stern tube and intermediate bearings across different states, both before and after offset adjustments.For the stern tube bearing, it is observed that the bearing reaction force increases slightly after the adjustments across all conditions, whereas the impact of the adjustment on the journal slope is more pronounced, as listed in Table 5.These changes indicate that recalibration of the vertical offset at the intermediate bearing aimed to redistribute the bearing loads, reducing the strain on the intermediate bearing.While slightly increasing the load on the stern tube bearing, maintaining it within the permissible load limits according to the class.The vertical offset adjustment significantly mitigated journal slope in the stern tube bearing, resulting in a notable improvement in alignment.As depicted in Table 5, the post-adjustment slopes were well within the permissible range.While the intermediate bearing experienced Fig. 6.Response of the controller to varying disturbance inputs minor slope changes, all values remained within acceptable limits.These findings suggest that the adjustments effectively enhanced the overall shafting system's alignment, particularly for the stern tube bearing.The targeted adjustment of the stern tube slope resulted in a consistent reduction across all operating conditions.In the drydocked cold fully immersed condition, the slope decreased from (0.4775 Mrad to 0.24377) Mrad.Similarly, improvements were observed in the afloat hot fully immersed (0.409 Mrad to 0.30083 Mrad) and afloat hot partially immersed (0.43014 Mrad to 0.28941 Mrad) conditions.All post-adjustment stern tube bearing slopes fell within the prescribed range of -0.30 to 0.30 Mrad, indicating successful alignment enhancement.Table 6 suggests that the adjustment in the vertical offset effectively enhanced the alignment of the intermediate bearing.The significant change in vertical offset, especially in the dry-docked cold fully immersed condition, is a positive indicator of improved alignment and reduced stress on the bearing components.Before the adjustment, the vertical offset was − 0.9 mm.After the adjustment, the offset decreased to -1.892 mm, indicating a substantial change, whilst it was less pronounced in the other two states.

Figure 8 demonstrates the performance of a PID-controlled intermediate bearing housing system operating under hydrodynamic conditions.A multi-frequency and double impulse disturbance model was employed to mimic practical scenarios, capturing the effects of disturbances on the bearing housing.

Under sinusoidal disturbance, the mathematical correction force (red line) begins at approximately 23.565 kN, reflecting a static correction based on the initial slope error.In contrast, the PID control force (blue dashed line) starts at a similar value but exhibits oscillations as the controller dynamically adjusts to counteract the slope error and external disturbances.Whereas for the impulse disturbance, the PID control force shows more pronounced oscillations in certain scenarios, suggesting the presence of higher disturbances and less optimal PID tuning.The slope dynamics reveal minimal steady-state error, indicating that the integral gain is effectively tuned to eliminate long-term errors.Overall, the PID controller successfully manages the slope error while adapting to dynamic system behavior and external disturbances.
Conclusion

A model of an automatic control system adjusting the bearing vertical offset of marine propeller shaft has been developed utilizing the shaft displacement and slope as the input and the intermediate bearing vertical displacement as the output to address the dynamic conditions of the ship in operation.Adjusting the intermediate bearing resulted in a notable alignment improvement, with a 50.83% enhancement in stern tube bearing alignment in the dry-docked state and a 32.7% improvement when afloat with partial propeller immersion.Implementing PID control for the actuation force on the intermediate bearing resulted in a new optimal elevation of − 0.076 mm (from − 0.9 mm), reducing the stern tube bearing slope to − 0.3 mrad under dynamic conditions.
